A predinner cocktail and dinner wine was also included. Bill was just under $4K including tip and was, if I do say so myself, one of the best wedding dinners I've eaten. After dinner anyone who wanted more "party" headed over to a pub and we drank beer until early hours. It was low-key, cheap(ish), and delicious, exactly what we wanted.

Dated for 5.5 years, engaged for 6 months. Invited probably 300 people, but had the wedding on a Wednesday night in January and knew a lot of people couldn't make it (that was partially intentional).

We were a bit older, so I'd like to think we had a better perspective on things. If I could pass a few things along.....

First, the wedding and reception aren't for you, they're for family. For those brides that think that it's "their day", it's not. By the time you get to the wedding, you're not going to care about much other than the major boxes getting checked off. Food? Cake? Music? Venue? Officiant? Get them checked off early and cheaply. At the end of the day, you'll have a handful of memories and NONE of them are going to be impacted by how much money you spent. I can tell you what I remember about my wedding. The look on my wife's face when I first saw her in her wedding dress. Her beautiful eyes as I choked up trying to repeat our vows. One of my groomsmen showing me a short, funny video before the wedding to think about in case I start crying (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UadhnOm2bp8, if you're interested). The look on my wife's face when she thought I would cram cake in her face (it still makes me smile). The dance with my mother. Cuddling up with her in bed the first night as officially husband and wife. Let me tell you what I don't remember about our wedding: What we had for a meal. What flavor our cake was. I remember our colors, only because I made fun of my wife that they were "wine and gold" and not "yellow and purple". I don't remember her dress, or her hair, or our music.

Speaking of cuddling...don't count on sex the night of your wedding. I don't mean that it won't happen. But understand, you're both going to be tired. It's a long day. If it happens, it happens; if it doesn't, it doesn't. You don't need any more pressure on you that day than you already have. Trying to plan a sexy wedding night shouldn't even be on the list. A buddy of mine and his wife waited for sex until they were married, then decided to push it on their wedding night...and he's regretted it ever since.

So, you're probably asking, what's for us then? THE HONEYMOON. The first thing we did after we set a date was booked our honeymoon. You know how I said you shouldn't try to plan a sexy wedding night? That's what the honeymoon is for. And take a while. We spent a week in Phoenix in January. It was amazing. We didn't plan anything (other than a bus day trip to the Grand Canyon). We found a cheap hotel and rental car, bought a coupon pack for Phoenix online, and bought a cheap printer in Phoenix that we donated to a charity when we left. We'd wake up every morning, look at each other, ask what the other wanted to do, then spent the day finding all the fun little nooks and crannies of Phoenix. We literally found places that even locals didn't know existed, and had a BLAST doing it. I may only have a few memories of the wedding, but the honeymoon I took a TON of memories away from the honeymoon.

tl;dr: Focus on what matters: it's the relationship, not the wedding.

I'm not sure what qualifies as our courtship period. We've known each other since 1998. In 1999, we dated for six months. But it didn't end well, so that doesn't seem like much of a courtship! The second time, over four years (and much emotional growth) later, we dated for about 10 months and then moved in together. I guess I should count those 10 months as the courtship!

Four years after that, we had a baby. Two years after that, I made a hypocrite out of myself and proposed to him. (I had spent the majority of my life being dead-set against marriage, but he wanted it so badly, so...) Three years later, we got married. Look, I'm an introvert and I also knew I would hate planning a wedding. So, it took three years for me to get comfortable with the idea.

We had a small wedding (about 60 guests) this past May. Sounds like everyone liked it, although I really would have preferred to elope to City Hall, but the groom wanted the whole shebang. So, I agreed to it as long as it was also a small shebang! Planning the wedding took 5 months. Five looong, stressful, why-the-fuck-did-I-agree-to-this months to plan a wedding that didn't even include a lot of the traditional trappings. (Unless you count the mother of the bride going completely insane, family butthurt, vendor fails, panicky bridal gown shopping, and various other traditional headaches.) I honestly don't know how people endure planning weddings for, like, a whole year.

The wedding took place in the afternoon on the patio of a well-known bar not far from our house, which is managed by a friend. Humanist minister. Music by my fiance's friends (all his friends are musicians), including a new song one of them wrote for the processional. Catered by a local bakery/cafe. No bridesmaids or groomsmen, just best man, maid of honour, flower girl, ring bearer (our son). Invitations created by my friend the book designer. We also did a lot ourselves; I made my own bouquet out of silk neckties, for example. I think the single biggest purchase we made was my dress. And it wasn't even supposed to work out that way. (Don't even get me started about the frantic search for a dress one month before the wedding!) We spent about $10,000 on the wedding, all told.

The wedding itself went off without a hitch. We even lucked out and got a summer-like day, even though the week leading up to it had been rainy and cool. But for me the best part of the day was when he and I went out for dinner by ourselves that night, still all dressed up. It was romantic. :)
